title: A patient at Camp Zama, Japan
description: Larry spent the rest of his service as a patient in Japan, very sick with what he called "sepititis", malaria and infections. He names the hospital himself: "I was at Camp Zama in Japan in Sugami Uro" — Sagami-Ōno, beside Camp Zama. His DD-214 lists his last duty assignment under the U.S. Army medical command in Japan, so he finished his service there as a patient, not on reassignment. He remembers arriving in early September and the weather turning cold, going into winter. In the hospital he befriended the man in the bed across from him, a fellow patient from back east, and on a pass the two of them went into Tokyo, to the Ginza. He does not remember the friend's name.
researchNotes: 2026-09-14: made distinct from the departure entry (1965-09-departure), which covers leaving Vietnam; this entry is his time as a patient in Japan, to separation on 30 November 1965 (1965-11-30-separation). sortDate is his own Camp Zama date ("may have been 9/3/1965", 2026-09-03-phone-camp-zama-date). Removed from the description the same day, as health detail (site audit): the symptoms he described in the 2026-08-12 call; they stay in his account (2026-call-japan-medevac.json) and ledger #7, and nothing was moved to private/. Also removed: the restaurant details of the Ginza day, which a standing interview question still asks about. Evidence: the clear DD-214 scan (2026-08-15, research/records-request/dd214-findings.md) reads the last-duty line as MHD, the medical holding unit that carried evacuated patients on the medical command's rolls, APO 96343 (Camp Zama); box 27 NONE. He named Camp Zama himself on 2026-08-13 when told only that research had a candidate (giscus-stories-c18006833). The AMEDD histories (cited) show the Camp Zama hospital was the Army's receiving hospital in Japan for Vietnam evacuees before December 1965, with 462 malaria admissions August–December 1965 (research/places/japan-hospital-1965.md). Not confirmed: no clinical record seen; NPRC clinical records are filed by hospital name. His "close to 4 months" (giscus-stories-c18118868) runs past the separation date; tensions and chain: research/events/medevac-chain-1965.md.
